hypothesis: The unannotated lipid-like feature with molecular formula C22H42N2O3 is increased/characteristic in 12-month-old infants relative to 5-month-old infants (i.e., increases across the complementary-feeding/weaning transition).
rationale: The feature is provided only as a molecular formula (C22H42N2O3, 3 degrees of unsaturation, 2 N, 3 O), with no compound name, HMDB/KEGG/LIPID MAPS identifier or spectral annotation. No publication located in this search reports a metabolite feature with this formula in infant stool/plasma, nor any age-related direction for it, so there is no study on this specific feature+group combination. Only formula-consistent class-level reasoning is available: the formula is compatible with bacterial/host N-acyl amide lipids such as an N-acyl lysine or N-acyl ornithine (e.g. a C16:1-lysine or C17:1-ornithine amide) or an N-acyl-amino-acid-type amide. For that broader class, human infant fecal metabolomics does support increases with age: the Cell Host & Microbe 2025 Bangladeshi mother-infant cohort explicitly reports that microbially derived N-acyl lipids and bile amidates rise with infant age as the microbiome matures, and other longitudinal infant fecal metabolome studies (first 1-2 years, including a complementary-feeding cohort sampled at ~4, 9 and 12 months) show that age/solid-food introduction is the dominant driver of fecal metabolome and lipid-metabolite shifts, with microbially derived amide/amino-acid-derived lipids becoming more prominent after weaning. This is generic/class- and pathway-level reasoning rather than direct evidence for this feature, and the direction of any individual N-acyl amide species can differ (some N-acyl amides are milk- or Bifidobacterium-associated and decline with weaning), so the evidence is supportive but weak and non-specific. Per the rubric this maps to 1 (weak): relevant literature was found, but nothing addresses this feature in this group, and the class-level evidence is only indirectly and partially applicable to an unidentified formula.

evidence.title: Environmental and maternal imprints on infant gut metabolic development
evidence.study_population: 55 Bangladeshi mother-infant dyads, longitudinal stool metagenomics + untargeted metabolomics over the first 6 months of life
evidence.relevance: Primary human infant study reporting that microbially derived N-acyl lipids (the compound class most consistent with a C22H42N2O3 amide, e.g. N-acyl lysine/ornithine) and bile amidates increase with infant age alongside microbiome maturation - class-level support for the hypothesized upward direction, though the cohort ends at 6 months and no C22H42N2O3 feature is named.

evidence.title: Environmental and Maternal Imprints on Infant Gut Metabolic Programming (preprint version)
evidence.study_population: Same Bangladeshi mother-infant cohort (n=55), first 6 months of life
evidence.relevance: Preprint of the above; confirms the reported age-associated increase in N-acyl lipids and bile amidates in infant stool, and links these to acquisition of microbial functions (bsh) after early infancy.

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Healthy infants sampled before solids (~4 months), at 9 months and at 12 months; paired 16S/shotgun and LC-MS aqueous + lipid fecal metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Directly spans the study's developmental window and shows that lipid-class fecal metabolites change markedly with complementary feeding, with lipid metabolite changes correlating with taxonomic shifts especially between 9 and 12 months - supports the plausibility of a lipid-amide feature being characteristic of 12-month stool, but does not identify C22H42N2O3.

evidence.title: Longitudinal profiles of the fecal metabolome during the first 2 years of life
evidence.study_population: Longitudinal infant fecal metabolome across the first 2 years of life
evidence.relevance: Shows age is a major driver of the infant fecal metabolome with several novel/unannotated metabolites and amino-acid-derived metabolites changing significantly with age - background support that many unannotated features increase between mid-infancy and 12 months, but no formula-level match.

evidence.title: Maturation of the gut metabolome during the first year of life in humans
evidence.study_population: Human infants followed to 12 months of age (fecal metabolome + microbiome)
evidence.relevance: Primary human study of fecal metabolome maturation to 12 months, documenting convergence and expansion of microbially derived metabolites (including acylcarnitines and amino-acid/vitamin pathways) by 12 months - contextual, class-level corroboration only.

evidence.title: Synthesis-driven reverse metabolomics reveals 3-hydroxy N-acyl amides as gut microbial molecules
evidence.study_population: Synthetic reference library plus untargeted metabolomics of human/microbial samples (not infant-specific)
evidence.relevance: Establishes that N-acyl amides of lysine and ornithine are genuine gut microbial molecules typically missing from spectral libraries, which is why a feature like C22H42N2O3 may remain unannotated; supports the candidate structural class but provides no infant age direction.

contradicting_evidence: No study reporting this formula/feature as decreased at 12 months versus 5 months was found. However, the direction is not uniform within the candidate compound class: several milk- and Bifidobacterium-linked amide/amino-acid-derived fecal metabolites (e.g. aromatic lactate and other breastfeeding-associated metabolites described in the SKOT/Bifidobacterium work) decline as breastfeeding stops, so an N-acyl amide of milk-fatty-acid origin (e.g. a C16:1 conjugate) could plausibly be higher at 5 months instead. This mixed picture is why the score is 1 rather than 2.

caveats: Identity is unresolved: C22H42N2O3 (RDBE 3) is consistent with multiple structures - N-acyl lysine (e.g. 16:1-lysine), N-acyl ornithine (e.g. 17:1-ornithine), other N-acyl amino acid amides, or even a non-biological amidopropyl-betaine-type surfactant/exogenous contaminant. Literature searches on a bare molecular formula are inherently low-yield, and all cited evidence is class-level rather than compound-specific. Confirmatory MS/MS annotation (e.g. against recent N-acyl amide spectral libraries) is needed before this hypothesis can be meaningfully scored; the strongest age-related N-acyl lipid evidence found covers 0-6 months rather than the 5- vs 12-month contrast, and none of it names this formula.
